question: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

Transhumance is a long-established pillar of rural Greece's production and environment, particularly in mountainous and disadvantaged areas. It helps preserve biodiversity and prevent rural depopulation and contributes to sustainable pasture management and the production of high-added-value products, such as Feta PDO. In Greece, tough restrictions have been introduced on the movement of herds to summer pastures, as a result of the sheep and goat pox epidemic. While the protection of animal health is absolutely necessary, livestock farmers practising seasonal transhumance are facing serious practical and financial challenges, namely high feed costs, difficulty in accessing pastures, additional transport and biosecurity costs, as well as uncertainty about the adequacy and speed of compensation. The issue is especially important given that the UN has declared 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, recognising the crucial role of pastoralism in food security, the resilience of rural communities and the protection of ecosystems. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is it monitoring the impact of sanitary restrictions on transhumance in Greece, particularly in mountainous and disadvantaged areas?
What European funding tools can be used right away to cover the increased costs of feed, transport, biosecurity and loss of access to pasture?
Does it intend to consider dedicated European initiatives, within the framework of the CAP and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists 2026, to support and maintain transhumance?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) 1. The Commission monitors the application of the Animal Health Law1 and remains in contact with the Greek authorities who are responsible for the implementation of sanitary restrictions. The Commission is also attentive to the broader effects that such restrictions may have on livestock farming systems, including transhumance practices. However, assessments of the socio-economic impact of these measures, including grazing activities, fall primarily within the competence of the Member States. 2. Support may be provided through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)2 Strategic Plans (CSP) including risk management and sectoral or investment-related measures3. In addition, exceptional measures are provided under Regulation (EU) No 1308/20134, to be funded by the agricultural reserve5. Support can also be granted by the national authorities to compensate for the costs of the prevention, control and eradication of animal diseases under the Agricultural de minimis Regulation6, the Agricultural Block Exemption Regulation (ABER)7 or the Agricultural state aid Guidelines8, provided that all relevant conditions are met. 3. Interventions for transhumance may be included in the CSPs notably as eco-schemes9. The Greek CSP provides for such an intervention10. The Commission will continue supporting awareness-raising and policy dialogue on sustainable agriculture, including transhumance, by
